questions.q: How does Brené Brown describe vulnerability itself?
a: Neither good nor bad; it is simply part of being human
A weakness that strong people learn to eliminate
A purely negative feeling that should be avoided
A skill that only trained leaders can develop
questions.why: Lesson 1 says vulnerability is not a black-and-white subject and is not inherently good or bad.

questions.q: Why does the summary call vulnerability the root of positive emotions too?
a: Loving someone means giving them the power to hurt you
Positive feelings only appear when you hide your true self
People who avoid risk feel more joy than others
Strong emotions can be felt without any connection
questions.why: Lesson 1 uses romantic love to show that openness brings both possible pain and deep joy.

questions.q: How can you take power away from shame, according to lesson 2?
a: Name what shames you and say it out loud
Keep it private until the feeling fades
Distract yourself with work and achievements
Compare your failure with worse failures
questions.why: Lesson 2 says pinpointing shame and expressing it reduces the hold it has over you.

questions.q: How do children acquire qualities, according to the summary?
a: By inheriting the qualities their parents actually live out
By being told which values are important
By attending schools with strict rules
By copying whatever their friends do
questions.why: Lesson 3 says children can only become who you are, so example matters more than talk.

questions.q: What does the summary say a family home should be?
a: A shame-free zone where children feel worthy and loved
A place where mistakes are punished quickly
A space focused mainly on academic achievement
A private area where emotions stay unspoken
questions.why: Lesson 3 says making home shame-free helps children grow up feeling worthy and able to be themselves.
